background.definition: Phimosis is the inability to retract the foreskin (prepuce) over the glans penis. It is divided up into physiologic and pathologic phimosis. Physiologic phimosis (vast majority of cases) is developmental nonretractability of the prepuce. Paraphimosis is an inability to return the foreskin to its original position over the glans penis, which subsequently leads to acute pain and edema of the glans.

list.listitem: Pathologic phimosis: 0.4 cases/1000 boys per year.
Phimosis: physiologic, balanitis, balanoposthitis, and balanitis xerotica obliterans.

Paraphimosis: iatrogenic from not returning foreskin to normal position such as after urination, bladder catheterization, examination or erection. It has also been associated with piercing of the glans.

Phimosis is most often physiologic. Pathologic phimosis occurs when there is distal scarring of the prepuce at the orifice. This scarring may be the result of infection (balanitis/balanoposthitis) or balanitis xerotica obliterans. Balanitis xerotica obliterans is a form of penile lichen sclerosis et atrophicus.
Paraphimosis occurs when the foreskin is retracted behind the glans penis causing constriction of the glans and edema. It may become a urologic emergency.
Paraphimosis can be effectively prevented by carefully replacing the foreskin over the glans after it is retracted for bladder catheterization, examination, or intercourse/erection. C
Suspect pathologic phimosis in boys who are 15 years and older, have evidence of scarring at the prepuce, or have painful erections. C
Suspect paraphimosis in patients with swelling of the distal glans with acute pain and edema. C
Diagnostic testing is not useful in the diagnosis of phimosis or paraphimosis. C

list.listitem: The term phimosis implies that tightness prevents the prepuce from being retracted by gentle manipulation. Most cases of phimosis in boys under the age of 15 years are physiologic.

If the patient has pathologic phimosis, he will have evidence of circumferential scarring of the prepuce at the orifice. Most cases of pathologic phimosis are due to balanitis xerotica obliterans. Pathologic phimosis in boys under the age of 5 is rarely if ever seen.

Patients with paraphimosis will be uncircumcised or partially circumcised males with pain, edema of the glans/distal penis, and a constricting band around the shaft of the penis usually caused by the foreskin. Items such as rings, bands, and piercings may also lead to paraphimosis.
See algorithm in .

A trial of a medium-potency steroid cream such as mometasone 0.1% applied twice daily to the prepuce for at least 4 weeks (or 0.05% betamethasone valerate cream applied twice daily for 8 weeks) should be considered in all patients with phimosis.,B
Patients with evidence of pathologic phimosis (scarring, painful erections, age 15 years and older) should be referred for possible surgical intervention such as circumcision. C

There are multiple techniques used to reduce paraphimosis. There is no clear evidence to show which is the best. Use of circumcision devices shortens operative time and may result in less short term pain and greater patient satisfaction.C

A randomized trial with 240 boys between the ages of 36 months and 13 years compared mometasone furoate 0.1% cream twice daily for 4 weeks with vehicle cream. They found an absolute risk reduction of 49% (NNT = 2). There are multiple nonrandomized trials that evaluate topical steroid creams all with similar results. The most frequently used treatments are medium-potency steroid creams such as betamethasone 0.05% or mometasone 0.1%.

A network meta-analysis identified 17 RCTs with 2057 participants with phimosis. Compared with control, they found that high potency (RR 3.2), moderate potency (RR 2.7) and low potency (RR 3.1) topical corticosteroids all increased the likelihood of partial or clinical resolution of phimosis to a similar degree.

A Cochrane review identified 14 RCTs with 1459 participants comparing topical corticosteroids with placebo or vehicle cream. They concluded that topical corticosteroids increase the likelihood of complete resolution at 4 to 8 weeks (688 vs 252 complete resolutions per 1000 boys, RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.8 to 4.2). Topical corticosteroids also increased the likelihood of partial resolution (501 vs 297 partial resolutiosn per 1000 boys,, RR 1.7, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.4).
One RCT of 52 children with a mean age = 4.6 years in the treatment group evaluated the use of diclofenac ointment in the treatment of phimosis (ARR 60%, NNT = 2).
There is limited research on treatment of phimosis in adults, but topical corticosteroids are probably safe and at least somewhat effective based on a systematic review of low quality evidence.

No RCTs are available evaluating the optimal treatment of paraphimosis. Pharmacologic methods to reduce paraphimosis include injection of hyaluronidase into the edematous prepuce. Most patients with paraphimosis will need pain control with a dorsal penile nerve block, topical anesthetic, or narcotics prior to reduction.
Surgical treatments of phimosis include circumcision and multiple other surgical techniques that spare the foreskin ("preputioplasty").

A network meta-analysis identified 18 RCTs with 6179 participants comparing different approaches to circumcision for patients with phimosis. They concluded that the disposable circumcision suture device was preferred.
Surgical treatments of paraphimosis include puncture methods and sharp incision of the constricting band. There are no RCTs that evaluate the most effective technique.

A Cochrane review of 18 randomized trials concluded that use of circumcision devices to perform circumcision shortens operative time and may result in less short term pain and greater patient satisfaction.
Most boys will need no treatment for phimosis, just time.

Paraphimosis can be reduced using one of several techniques. These include application of granulated sugar for 2 hours, application of ice to the area for 5 minutes, or application of an elastic bandage around the penis for 5 to 7 minutes or until the edema subsides. All of these methods are aimed at reducing the edema associated with the paraphimosis.
Manual reduction has also been described in the literature.

Patients with evidence of pathologic phimosis should be referred for surgical intervention. Findings consistent with pathologic phimosis include scarring at the orifice of the prepuce, painful erections, or age 15 years and older. Children under the age of five rarely have pathologic phimosis and therefore will rarely need surgical intervention.
Paraphimosis may become a urological emergency. If reduction of paraphimosis fails using less invasive techniques, a surgical consultation should be obtained immediately.

Children with phimosis may have "ballooning." This is when the foreskin blocks the urethral meatus and urine collects between the foreskin and glans. This is not dangerous and the urine will usually drain without intervention. This is not an indication for circumcision.
Fournier's gangrene has been reported as a very rare but serious complication.
Rate of nonretractile foreskin is 80% at 6 months, 10% at 3 years, 8% at 6 years, and 1% at 16 years. B
Most cases of phimosis are physiologic and do not require surgical intervention such as circumcision. C
Paraphimosis may lead to necrosis of the distal penis in some instances. B

Boys younger than 15 years who are diagnosed with phimosis should be followed yearly for resolution of the phimosis. If evidence of scarring, pain with erection, recurrent infection, or inflammation occur, the child should be referred for possible surgical intervention such as circumcision. C

There is an association between a history of phimosis and and increased risk for penile cancer, but this is likely confounded by other clinical variables including sexually transmitted infections, socioeconomic factors, and circumcision.
Paraphimosis in elderly men may be complicated by other medical conditions such as diabetes. These patients may have underlying neuropathy and may not have pain associated with paraphimosis.
Phimosis is usually a physiologic condition that resolves with age. While it is very common in children younger than 3 years, it is rare in men older than 15 yeras.
